title: Evan Bouchard's Hot Start Is Real, But the Goals Will Cool
dek: The Oilers defenseman leads all blueliners in points, but seven goals on 2.5 expected tells us where the next few weeks may go.
text:
Evan Bouchard has 22 points in 13 games, the most of any defenseman in the league. That is the headline, and it is a fair one. It is also only part of the picture, because the way those points have arrived says as much about his season as the total does.

## Who he is

Bouchard is 27, born in Oakville, Ontario, a right-shot defenseman listed at 6'2" and 196 pounds. Edmonton took him 10th overall in the 2018 draft out of the London Knights. Central Scouting's final ranking had him fourth among North American skaters, so the Oilers got him a little later than the ranking suggested. Vitali Kravtsov went one pick earlier and Oliver Wahlstrom one pick later.

His last stop before the NHL was a big one: 87 points, 25 of them goals, in 67 OHL games for London in 2017-18. By our league translation, which converts junior production into an estimate of NHL scoring, that is worth roughly 31 points over 82 NHL games. It is a conservative number, and he has beaten it comfortably. Last season he scored 95 points (21 goals, 74 assists) in 82 games. Internationally he played for Canada at the 2015 U17 World Challenge (6 points in 6 games), the 2016 Hlinka Gretzky Cup and the 2019 World Juniors, where he had 3 points in 5 games.

He has spent his entire career in Edmonton, 442 games now, with 83 goals and 272 assists for 355 points. He is an alternate captain.

## How he's being talked about

The conversation around him right now is about the Norris Trophy. The headlines from the past few days are almost all one story. Yahoo Sports led with "McDavid Makes Bold Claim About Bouchard Ahead Of Prime Matchup vs. Flames," and Markerzone.com reported that Oilers captain Connor McDavid told Amazon Prime that Bouchard deserved the Norris. NHL Trade Talk framed it as McDavid calling out award voters for a snub. The New York Times asked on October 24 what it would take for Bouchard to win the trophy, and The Oil Rig wondered whether he can become the seventh defenseman in NHL history to hit 100 points in a season.

CBS Sports noted an eight-game, 13-point scoring streak on October 25. ClutchPoints covered his overtime winner against Minnesota, a goal he scored on his birthday. So the mood around him is hype, and it is backed by production. The question for us is how much of that production is sustainable.

## What the season looks like

The raw line is 7 goals and 15 assists in 13 games, with 7 of the 22 points coming on the power play. He is averaging 26.17 minutes a game, sixth among defensemen, and over his last 10 games that has climbed by 1.63 minutes per game to 26.31. In those 10 games he has 14 points, a little ahead of the 12.8 our model expected.

The team has been good: EDM is 9-2-2 and controls 52.8% of the expected goals, which measures the quality of chances rather than just goals. With Bouchard on the ice, the team's share of expected goals at five-on-five is 60.25%, a strong number. The Oilers have also scored 14.58 more goals than expected while he is on the ice, which is a lot of finishing luck spread across everyone he plays with.

His game log has some rough nights inside the streak. In the 2-7 loss to Toronto he had two assists. Against Carolina he took no shots but set up a goal in a 6-5 win. Three times he has played more than 28 minutes (31.7 against Detroit in an overtime loss). Those are the minutes of a defenseman the coaching staff leans on.

## What is really driving it

Here is where it gets interesting. Bouchard's own expected goals this season are 2.5, the eighth-highest among defensemen. He has scored 7. That is 4.5 goals above what his chances would predict, and he is shooting 18% against 10% last season. We flagged him as due to cool for that reason. The chances are real, but a finishing rate that high rarely holds.

His shot map explains why the chances are modest in quality. Of his 63 unblocked shots, 55 came from beyond 30 feet, producing 5 goals on 1.6 expected. Eight came from 15 to 30 feet (2 goals on 0.9 expected), and none from inside 15 feet. His average shot distance is 51.3 feet. He is a point shooter. The busiest area is the right point, with 16 shots on goal and one goal, followed by six from the center point. The tracking data shows why those shots still work: his hardest shot is 94.8 mph, in the 92nd percentile. His top skating speed is 21.5 mph (71st percentile), with six bursts over 20 mph.

The hand-tracked numbers from All Three Zones (Corey Sznajder), which cover 24 tracked games and 418.2 five-on-five minutes from 2025-26, fill in the rest. He ranks in the 97th percentile for primary shot assists (7.17 per 60 minutes against a league typical 4) and the 99th for chance assists (3.87 against 1.57). He carries the puck in on 59% of his zone entries, the top mark among defensemen and more than double the typical 28%. This is a defenseman who creates offense for others, which is why the assists are less fluky than the goals. One quirk: he gets no shots off high-danger passes (14th percentile), which fits a player who shoots from distance.

Evolving-Hockey's models tell the same story over the long run. They credit him with 3.3 wins above replacement last season (5th among 215 defensemen), including +14.3 goals from even-strength offense and +6.5 on the power play. The defensive side is a mild negative: -2.7 goals at even strength, and he ranks in the 33rd percentile for limiting chances against. He draws more penalties than he takes, worth +2.6 goals. The model also notes he plays with strong teammates (93rd percentile), which flatters his raw on-ice numbers.

Our own model blends this season with last and with his role, because 13 games is too few to trust alone. It puts his expected goal rate at 0.44 per 60, the same as last year, and sees him getting a point on 51% of the goals scored while he is on the ice.

## What to watch

The shooting percentage is the thing to track. If he keeps scoring at 18% on shots from 50 feet, the goals will stay ahead of the chances, but history says they won't. A drift toward 10% would take some goals off the ledger without changing how well he plays. The assists should hold up better, since his passing and carrying numbers rank so high.

The 100-point talk is the other watch item. He had 95 last year, and at the current pace he would sail past that, though 13 games is a small sample and much of this run is finishing luck.

What would change the picture? Defensive numbers that improve, which would make his case for the Norris stronger than the point totals alone. A drop in ice time would be a warning that the staff is managing him. Continued scoring from beyond 30 feet would mean something has changed in his shot or his screens. For now, we'd call him a very good defenseman running hot, and expect the goals to come back toward the chances.
